q.intro.text: A new freezer is switched on at fifty degrees Fahrenheit. It cools six degrees every hour.

q.ask.text: After h hours it is fifty minus six h degrees. For which hours is it colder than eight degrees? That is, fifty minus six h is less than eight.

e.intro.text: Four steps. Press each one: the number lines move first, then the notation.

e.s1.text: The top line holds temperatures. Fifty minus six h must be below eight: an open dot at eight, because eight degrees is not colder than eight degrees, shaded to the left.

e.s2.text: Subtract fifty from both sides. Every number slides fifty to the left: the arrows run side by side, and nothing passes anything. Negative six h is less than negative forty-two: the symbol stays.

e.s3.text: Divide both sides by negative six. The arrows cross: dividing by a negative mirrors every number through zero, so the order turns around. h is greater than seven.

e.s4.text: Test it. h equals nine: fifty minus fifty-four is negative four, and negative four is less than eight. Check. h equals five: fifty minus thirty is twenty, not less than eight. So the ray is on the right side: h is greater than seven.

e.why.text: Quick check: why did less than turn into greater than?

e.w-ok.text: Yes. A negative factor swaps the order of every pair of numbers, so the symbol has to turn too.

e.w-neg.text: A minus sign showing is not the reason. Subtracting fifty had a minus too, and the symbol stayed.

e.w-sub.text: Look at the first move: the arrows ran side by side, and the symbol stayed. Only the division by negative six turned it.

t.intro.text: Your turn: negative three x plus four is less than or equal to nineteen. The first two steps are done for you.

t.land.text: Now divide both sides by negative three. Where does fifteen land? Fifteen divided by negative three is what?

t.l-ok.text: Yes: fifteen divided by negative three is negative five. The boundary lands on negative five. Watch where the other numbers go.

t.l-sign.text: Dividing a positive by a negative gives a negative: fifteen divided by negative three is negative five, not five.

t.l-no.text: What times negative three makes fifteen? That is where fifteen lands.

t.sym.text: The arrows crossed. Which is the solution set?

t.s-ok.text: Yes: the order turned, and the or equal stays. x is greater than or equal to negative five.

t.s-keep.text: Look at the arrows: they crossed, so the ray turns around.

t.s-incl.text: Turning the symbol keeps the or equal: negative five itself still works.

t.s-only.text: Negative five is only the boundary. A whole ray of numbers works.

t.test.text: Test a value on the other side: x equals negative seven. What is negative three times negative seven, plus four?

t.t-ok.text: Twenty-five. Is twenty-five less than or equal to nineteen? No: negative seven is not a solution, just as x greater than or equal to negative five says. And x equals negative three gives thirteen, which is less than nineteen. Check.

t.t-sign.text: A negative times a negative is positive: negative three times negative seven is twenty-one. Then add four.

t.t-no.text: Multiply first: negative three times negative seven is twenty-one, then add four.

t.cb-right.text: At the start you picked h greater than seven, and you were right. Now you can show why: the arrows cross when you divide by a negative.

t.cb-keep.text: At the start you picked h less than seven. That keeps the symbol, but dividing by negative six turns it: after seven hours the freezer is colder than eight degrees.

t.cb-only.text: At the start you picked h equals seven. At seven hours it is exactly eight degrees, not colder. Every time after that works: h is greater than seven.

t.cb-none.text: Find the boundary, carry the symbol through every step, and turn it only when you multiply or divide by a negative.

p.intro.text: Jordan solves two x minus five is greater than negative eleven. Add five: two x is greater than negative six. Divide by two: x is less than negative three. Jordan says: I turned the symbol because the numbers are negative. Is Jordan right?

p.test.text: Let’s test it. Build the argument, and see where it leads.

p.prove.text: Now prove it. Fill each because with the reason that makes the line true.

p.c1.text: Adding five to both sides keeps the order: two x is greater than negative six,

p.c2.text: dividing both sides by two keeps it too: x is greater than negative three,

p.c3.text: so Jordan’s answer, x less than negative three, is wrong,

p.x-neg.text: A negative number showing is not a reason. Only multiplying or dividing by a negative turns the symbol.

p.x-add.text: Look at the arrows for plus five: they run side by side. Adding never turns the order.

p.x-only.text: Negative three is only the boundary. The question is which side of it works.

p.x-one.text: One test that works is not enough. Test a value in Jordan’s set too.

p.x-other.text: True, but it is the reason for a different line.

p.done.text: That’s a proof: three claims, each with its reason, and the number lines back every one. Jordan turned the symbol without dividing by a negative.
